theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids
notes: Indra 'who drove out the cattle' from Vala (RV 2.12.3, 8.14.8); Hercules driving Geryon's cattle in Latium before Cacus steals them (Vergil, Livy: not in the local Latin corpus, which has Cato's boues ... ages only in a farming context, Agr. 72); Old Irish táin bó 'driving of cattle' (táin < *to-ag-), the name of the cattle-raid genre (West ch. 12). Accusative plural *gʷṓms = Ved. gā́ḥ. Past of the present stem with the Vedic imperfect; Latin has imperfect and perfect. The Vedic preverb úd 'out' is left out (Vedic only). Greek uses ἐλαύνω (*h₁elh₂-) with βοῦς instead (Hes. Th. 291, Il. 1.154).

theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids
notes: Saramā's threat to the cattle-thieving Paṇis, 'slain by Indra, o Paṇis, you will lie' (RV 10.108.4), which Watkins (ch. 53) sets beside Hekabe's 'newly slain you lie' (πρόσφατος ... κεῖσαι, Il. 24.757): *gʷʰn̥tó- + 2nd person middle of *ḱey- in both, with Avestan 'they lie slain' (Yt. 10.80). Number: Vedic plural (the Paṇis), Greek singular; the plural is kept for the cattle-raid setting. 'By Indra' (índreṇa) is left out (no lexeme).

theme: Storm and Stream: Viśvarūpa and his cows
Arms and the Man: Cattle raids

plan.english: I will drive off the two women.

notes: Watkins ch. 48: in the Iranian form of the Viśvarūpa/Geryon myth the cattle are replaced by women; Θraētaona asks to 'carry off' Aži Dahāka's two wives, with az- used of booty as of cattle, and Avestan azāni (1sg subjunctive) is identical to Agamemnon's κ' ἄγω Βρισηΐδα (Il. 1.184): *h₂éǵoh₂. 'Woman' (gʷḗn) is interpolated (Av. vaṇta 'the two beloved', Gk. the name Briseis); the dual follows the Avestan.

theme: Storm and Stream: Viśvarūpa and his cows
Arms and the Man: Cattle raids

plan.english: Three heads were his. He slew him, and drove off his cattle.

notes: Watkins ch. 48: HERO SLAY THREE-HEADED MONSTER, DRIVE OFF his COWS (Trita/Indra and Viśvarūpa; Herakles and Geryon). Secure: 'three' (Ved. tri-, Gk. τρι-) and *gʷṓws (Ved. gā́ḥ, Gk. βοῦς, Lat. boves). *gʷʰen- is Vedic only here (Hesiod has ἐξενάριξε, Livy interimo); 'drive' is *h₂eǵ- with Latin abigo (Greek ἐλαύνω, Vedic ā-kṛ); 'head' differs (Ved. śīrṣán-, Gk. -κέφαλος). The compound 'three-headed' is rendered by a clause with the dative of possession (as Gk. κεφαλαὶ δέ οἱ ἦσαν τρεῖς, Il. 11.39). Hesiod and Livy are not in the local corpora.

theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids

plan.english: If anyone steals a head of cattle, he shall give six cattle.

notes: Cattle theft in law and curse: Hittite Laws §67 'if anyone steals a cow ... now he gives six cattle' (tāyezzi); RV 7.104.10 curses 'whoever (harms) our horses, our cattle ... the thief' (stená-). Secure is the root *(s)teh₂- 'steal' (Hitt. tāye-, Ved. stená-, tāyú-); the Hittite cattle are written with the logogram GU₄, so *gʷṓws counts as Vedic only. Indefinite *kʷis 'anyone' (Hitt. kuiški) and 'give' (*deh₃-, aorist subjunctive for the legal future; Hitt. pai- is not cognate) are interpolated.

theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids

plan.english: They did not drive off my cattle and horses.

notes: Achilles: the Trojans never raided 'my cattle nor my horses' (Il. 1.154); the Paṇis' hoard that Indra's party comes to raid is 'filled with cattle, with horses' (RV 10.108.7). Shared: *gʷṓws and *h₁éḱwos as the pair of raidable wealth. The verb is the Greek *h₁elh₂- (aorist ἤλασαν = h₁élh₂t), Greek only; 'my' and the negation are Greek only. Greek has 'never' (πώποτε); the line has plain 'not'.

theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids

plan.english: He drives the cattle of the enemy.

notes: Raiding the stranger's herds: Indra 'drives together the cattle of the stranger, of whom he wishes' (RV 1.33.3); Nestor's raid on the Eleans, 'we drove together ... fifty herds of cattle' (Il. 11.677-678). Shared: *gʷṓws, and the root *h₂eǵ- (Ved. ajati; Gk. ἀγέλη 'herd, what is driven'; the Greek verb is ἐλαύνω). 'Enemy' is gʰóstis (gloss 'guest; stranger, enemy'), standing for Ved. arí- 'stranger' (not cognate); the preverbs sám/συν- are left out.

theme: Arms and the Man: Cattle raids
notes: Indra 'you won the cattle, hero' (RV 1.32.12, after the slaying of Vṛtra, likening the freed waters to the cows held by the Paṇi in 1.32.11); Nestor's account of the raid on the Eleans, with its herds of cattle (Il. 11.677) and 'the might of Herakles' (βίη Ἡρακληείη, 11.690) that had wasted Pylos. Shared: *gʷṓws and the root *gʷey- 'win by force' (Ved. jáyati, imperfect ájayaḥ; Gk. βίη is the action noun, lexeme gʷeyós). 2nd person singular with no vocative: the addressee (Indra) has no lexeme. The lexeme gʷéyeti has a derived gloss ('to win, to conquer').
